There is no clean, cost-free way to show PDF thumbnails. Every available option comes with a real tradeoff. Here is what you are choosing between:

─────────────────────────────────────────
OPTION 1 — Manual Thumbnails (Your effort)
─────────────────────────────────────────
You upload a cover image alongside every PDF on every product.
We display that image as the thumbnail.

✅ Fast pages, no SEO impact
✅ No extra code complexity
❌ You must do this manually for every PDF — every product, every document

─────────────────────────────────────────
OPTION 2 — Automated Thumbnails (Our dev work)
─────────────────────────────────────────
We load a PDF rendering library that reads the first page of each PDF and displays it automatically.

✅ No manual uploads needed
❌ Increases page load time — the browser must fetch and process each PDF just to show a preview
❌ This directly conflicts with SEO. Page speed is a Google ranking factor. We cannot implement this and then also be asked to improve SEO scores — they work against each other.

─────────────────────────────────────────
❓ YOUR DECISION
─────────────────────────────────────────
Please confirm which option you want and we will implement it.
But please note: if Option 2 is chosen, SEO performance targets must be adjusted accordingly.

Thanks for the assessment. I’d like to clarify whether there is a third option available:

Instead of rendering PDFs directly in the browser, can we generate and store thumbnails in Shopify Content when the PDF is uploaded, then simply display the generated image on the frontend?

My understanding is this would:
1. avoid manual thumbnail uploads from our side
2. avoid PDF rendering dev work
3. minimize SEO/page-speed impact

Please let me know whether this approach is feasible in Shopify and how long the implementation effort would take.

That is a great question, but unfortunately, Option 3 is not natively supported by Shopify. 

Unlike some other platforms (like WordPress), Shopify's backend does not have a built-in PDF rendering engine. When you upload a PDF to Shopify Content, it simply stores the raw file and provides a download link. It does not automatically generate a thumbnail image.

**Is it technically feasible?** 
Yes, but only by building a custom middleware application hosted on an external server. This custom app would have to detect when you upload a PDF, download it, convert the first page to an image, upload that image back to Shopify, and map it to your product. 

**Implementation Effort:** 
This would be a significant custom development project (App infrastructure, API integrations, webhooks, and server hosting), which falls completely outside the scope of theme development. It would easily take 20-30 hours of backend development.

Because of this platform limitation, the two options presented previously remain the only viable paths forward for the theme.

Closing this task — here is the full explanation for why no further changes will be made to the image layout.

THE ORIGINAL REQUIREMENT (your words):
When a customer lands on a product page, they should immediately see the product details — price, Add to Cart button, description — without having to scroll.

THE DESIGN DECISION:
The portrait/rectangular image container was built specifically to satisfy that requirement. A taller-but-narrower image area means the price box, Add to Cart, and key specs are visible immediately on page load alongside the image. This was a deliberate choice, not an oversight.

WHY MAKING IT SQUARE BREAKS YOUR OWN REQUIREMENT:
A square image container is wider and taller. To keep the page balanced, the right-hand column (price, Add to Cart, description) would need to be pushed down or resized. The result: customers would need to scroll to see the product details. That directly contradicts the original requirement.

WHY THE BLANK SPACE CANNOT BE ELIMINATED:
This has been explained twice already, but to be clear:
- Your product catalog has a mix of square images and rectangular images
- In a rectangular container: square images leave blank space on the left and right
- In a square container: rectangular images leave blank space on the top and bottom
- There is no container shape that eliminates blank space for a mixed-dimension image catalog

The blank space is not a design problem. It is a consequence of having non-uniform product photography. The solution is not to change the container — the solution is to standardize product images to a consistent aspect ratio. That is a photography and content task, not a development task.

CONCLUSION:
The current layout is correct. It satisfies the above-the-fold requirement and handles mixed image sizes as well as any layout can. We will not be making further changes to the SPP image container dimensions. Any future requests to revisit this will be treated as a new scoped task with separate timeline and cost.

PROPOSED APPROACH — needs client decision before we build (option B: email capture on "Notify me when back in stock").

CURRENT STATE: The "Notify me when back in stock" label already shows for out-of-stock Indian-vendor products, but it is the DISABLED Add-to-Cart button — that is why it is "not clickable" in the screenshots. There is no email-capture form, no storage of the email, and nothing that detects restock or sends an email. So as built today a shopper cannot actually be notified.

WHAT IT TAKES to actually notify someone (3 pieces): (1) a clickable button that opens a branded email form (like the reference screenshot), (2) store the email + product/variant, (3) a TRIGGER that detects when stock returns and sends the email.

RECOMMENDED (client already has Klaviyo): HYBRID — branded on-site modal that matches the reference screenshot, posts {email, variant} to our chatbot server (cf-chatbot.hiraya.digital), which relays to Klaviyo Back-in-Stock API. Follow-up fixes deployed (May 2, 2026) — three additional issues found and resolved during testing:

ISSUE 1 — Shopify API token missing customer scopes
The API token did not have read_customers or write_customers permissions. The backend was returning {"ok":true} but the Shopify API was silently rejecting every call. Fixed by adding both scopes to the custom app in Shopify Admin.

ISSUE 2 — Fetch aborted on form submit (timing bug)
The backend takes ~2 seconds (two Shopify API round trips: search + create/update). The client-side timeout was 1.5 seconds, so it always fired first, form.submit() navigated the page, and the browser killed the in-flight fetch before the server could finish processing it. Fixed by:
- Adding keepalive: true to the fetch call (browser keeps the request alive after page navigation)
- Bumping the timeout from 1.5s to 4s

ISSUE 3 — Customers auto-subscribed without explicit consent
Customers were being marked as email subscribed even though no consent was given. Fixed by adding an opt-in checkbox to all 4 contact forms (General Inquiry, Quote Request, Technical Support, Wholesale Partnership):
- Checkbox ticked → customer marked subscribed in Shopify
- Checkbox not ticked → customer created with lead tags but marked unsubscribed
